<reason>Both sides were sharp, but PRO built the cleaner decision rule and kept it live to the end. PRO's opening frame (harassment as a selection mechanism deciding who gets to be spontaneous) was never dislodged, and PRO's rebuttal that CON's examples (throwaways, brigading, dumb filters) describe under-resourced enforcement rather than over-enforcement was a strong turn. CON's best move was the "precision vs. aggression are different knobs" distinction plus the identity-verification tax on vulnerable players, and CON scored a real hit by getting PRO to say "Yes" to turning up automated filtering. But PRO answered directly (aggression = consequence and speed on confirmed cases, appeals at the edges; friction only after a strike, not on day one), and CON's insistence that this is "not the motion" relied on defining aggression narrowly as only cheap automation. Decisively, CON never gave a satisfying answer to what happens to the proven slur-spammer: "loses his audience" via reputation-weighted matchmaking is itself report-driven central moderation—the very instrument CON attacked—and CON's closing reframe of that question as mere "retribution" read as evasive on the motion as written. CON also had two clipped turns and slightly misdescribed A4.3. PRO's closing ("one system occasionally punishes the wrong player and fixes it; the other never punishes the right one") made the choice easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 1 turning every CON example into evidence of under-enforcement ([A2.2]–[A2.6]), reinforced by the unanswered Q2 pressure on what consequence the abuser faces; CON's "different knobs" counter ([B2.1]) was the strongest reply but PRO's A1 definition of aggression as consequence/speed on confirmed cases largely absorbed it.</best_rebuttal>
